articles.title: South Africa police launch manhunt after 17 killed in tavern shooting
articles.summary: South African police launched a manhunt Sunday after 17 people were killed and 15 wounded in a shooting in a township outside Johannesburg.
articles.body: South African police launched a manhunt Sunday after 17 people were killed and 15 wounded in a shooting in a township outside Johannesburg. Police said eight unidentified men opened fire on patrons drinking outside the tavern in Wedela, West Rand District on Saturday evening local time, before they entered the establishment and “continued shooting at patrons inside.” The alleged assailants were reportedly armed with pistols and AK-47 rifles, officers said. Fifteen people with gunshot wounds had been transferred to medical facilities for treatment. “It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside. The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside,” South Africa police wrote on X. The attackers allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. No arrests have been made at this stage, police said. Mass shootings are not uncommon in South Africa. Last week 11 people, including a woman believed to be pregnant, were killed when gunmen opened fire at a house south of the city of Durban. In June, 12 people were killed at an informal settlement in a Johannesburg suburb. The latest police figures show that an average of 58 people were murdered each day in South Africa between January and March. This is a developing story and will be updated. Nimi Princewill contributed reporting.

articles.title: Lifeguard patrols reduced at Devon, Cornwall and Jersey beaches
articles.summary: The RNLI says as the summer season has finished some sites will move to weekend-only cover.
articles.body:
Beachgoers are being reminded that lifeguard patrol times are set to change as the summer season ends.

The RNLI said patrols would change at beaches across Devon, Cornwall and Jersey in the coming weeks, with some sites moving to weekend-only cover, and encouraged anyone visiting the coast to choose a lifeguarded beach and check the conditions before heading into the water.

RNLI regional lifeguard lead Henry Saddler-Irvine thanked lifeguards and support teams for their work during what he described as a busy summer.

"They have demonstrated professionalism, resilience and teamwork every day, often in challenging conditions, to help keep people safe along our coastline," he said.

The RNLI said weekend-only patrols would operate on Bantham, Croyde and Woolacombe beach in Devon between 28 September to 18 October and during the October half-term.

In Cornwall, weekend-only patrols would operate across the same time period on Tregonhawke, Praa Sands, Crantock, Towan, Watergate Bay, Mawgan Porth, Porthtowan, Chapel Porth, Gwithian North, Hayle Towans, Constantine, Harlyn, Polzeath, Widemouth and Summerleaze.

Full-time daily patrols will continue until 1 November at Fistral, Perranporth, Porthmeor and Sennen.

In Jersey, weekend-only patrols will operate on Le Braye between 28 September to 18 October and during the October half-term.

articles.title: Bumblebee project seeking to 'turn the tide' for rare UK species
articles.summary: The programme to help the Moss carder species will focus on Cornwall, Kent and the North Pennines.
articles.body:
A project is under way to try and help one of the UK's "most threatened" species of bumblebee.

The Bumblebee Conservation Trust is leading a £907,000 three-year scheme alongside the University of Cambridge to recover the Moss carder species.

It said the initiative would focus on landscapes across Cornwall's coastal grasslands, dunes and heathland as well as grazing marshes and sea walls in Kent and the upland fringe landscape of the North Pennines.

During the project, the trust said it would work with landowners to trial "small-scale habitat interventions" to identify those which work well while gaining a better understanding of the species' behaviour and needs.

Moss carder bumblebees are largely found in small, fragmented populations, according to the trust.

It said it was distinctive with a velvety covering of ginger-yellow hairs across its body and no black hairs.

The trust said habitat loss and fragmentation were likely to have a bigger impact on the Moss carder than many other species as it typically foraged closer to its nest than most other bumblebees.

Amy Plowman, head of conservation and science at the trust, said: "This is a hugely exciting and ambitious three-year project that gives us a real opportunity to turn the tide for one of the UK's rarest bumblebees."

Funding worth more than £530,000 has been provided to the project by Natural England's Species Recovery Programme.

Tylan Berry, Natural England's species and nature recovery networks senior officer, said the Species Recovery Programme was helping "take practical action to halt species decline and support nature recovery across England".

Berry said the Moss carder was "one of England's most threatened pollinators".

"Projects like this demonstrate how targeted investment can support practical conservation action on the ground," he added.

articles.title: Heat and drought put record demand on Devon fire service
articles.summary: The fire service says it dealt with 'sustained levels of demand in challenging conditions'.
articles.body:
Firefighters faced "record-breaking" demand over the summer, responding to more than 2,000 incidents in one month alone, a fire service has said.

Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue said prolonged hot and dry weather led to sustained and unprecedented levels of demand, particularly in July.

The service said control room staff handled 6,041 calls during the month, while firefighters attended 2,008 incidents, including 864 fires. Of those, 547 were classed as open-air fires.

Kate Saint, the service's head of prevention, said it dealt with "sustained levels of demand in challenging conditions", adding "many people changed their behaviour as the risk increased".

The service said from 8 July onwards there was "exceptionally high demand and the "pace of activity was relentless".

It said it wanted to recognise those who responded to the increased risk by postponing barbecues and taking "extra care" with outdoor heat sources.

The service said autumn and winter would bring different challenges, including flooding, storms, colder weather and an increased risk of fires in the home. It said it would monitor the El Niño event and prepare accordingly.

It urged residents to ensure smoke alarms are working, have chimneys and flues swept before using open fires or wood burners, and take extra care on the roads during wet and darker conditions.

The fire service also warned people to stay away from open water after drinking alcohol, particularly after nights out.

articles.title: Music sessions for Guernsey pupils with additional needs
articles.summary: Organisers hope the inclusive sessions will help to increase confidence and improve social skills.
articles.body:
A new music initiative designed to support pupils with additional learning needs has been launched in Guernsey.

Pupils from Le Rondin School will take part in the programme, called Music Makers, which has been launched by the Guernsey Youth Commission and Guernsey Music Centre with sponsorship from law firm Collas Crill.

Organisers said it had been tailored for children with neurodiversity, physical disabilities and communication differences in an inclusive environment.

The youth commission's chief executive, Lou Leale, said music could help children with additional learning needs express themselves, develop confidence and build social connections.

"We hope that, through regular participation, children will develop increased confidence, improved engagement with peers and adults, stronger communication and social skills, and a greater sense of belonging," Leale said.

Tim Wright, head of the Guernsey Music Service, said the funding from Collas Crill would enable specialist teachers to deliver "high-quality music education outside of school".

The funding would cover staffing costs, musical instruments and related equipment needed to deliver the programme, he said.

Kim Halliwell, the firm's group head of marketing and communications, said: "Our aim in any local sponsorship is to help create opportunities for people to shine.

"The Music Makers sessions do just that and we're delighted to be supporting the Youth Commission and the Music Service to help remove barriers and bring joy through the magic of music."

The sessions would will run alongside existing music centre groups on Saturdays, organisers said.

articles.title: Traitors star burgled after sharing photos while on holiday
articles.summary: Paul Gorton urges people to think twice before sharing holiday pictures before they are back home.
articles.body:
Traitors star Paul Gorton did not think twice about sharing photographs on social media while enjoying a family holiday with his wife and two young children.

But when he returned home he discovered that his house in Cheshire had been burgled just days earlier.

"The eerie bit is at 21:10 BST I posted that me and Kate were by the side of the pool, we've got full bellies, the kids are in bed, we're actually having our little bit of the holiday," he said.

"About 20 minutes later, little did we know, our house has been broken into."

Paul's bike as well as several sentimental items including an irreplaceable ring from Kate's grandmother were stolen in the burglary on 28 August.

The perpetrators managed to break in through the bi-fold doors at the back of the house by using a technique known as lock snapping before cutting the broadband connection.

Paul, who was a contestant on the second series of the popular BBC series, said he reported the burglary to Cheshire Police, with the force describing it as a "one-off hit".

As a result, Paul believes it was a "targeted attack".

"They said they normally see people come in from far and wide and they [target] a couple of houses in a night but this isn't the case," said Paul, who is originally from St Helens.

"This makes me suspect that it could be someone that follows me.

"They've seen that I've posted that I was away and then thought 'let's go in the house and see if we can get ourselves some goodies'."

Paul said he hoped other people would learn from his misfortune.

"I think the key message is for people to be a little bit smarter, more conscientious when they're posting and post when they're back at home.

"Hopefully people can learn from my mistakes.

"I guess the aim is the worst thing that's happened to us could be the best thing that will happen to you because you can protect yourself moving forward and that's the whole reason behind the campaign."

Following the burglary, Paul has joined forces with Compare the Market, which commissioned a licensed private investigator to examine the publicly available digital footprints of nine volunteers.

They were able to identify seven home addresses by using publicly available information.

The fastest home address was identified in 15 minutes, with the first lead found in only 50 seconds.

"It's not just about social media," said Paul.

"I've learned to think about the whole picture with locks, alarms, lights, what you're posting online and whether you're accidentally advertising that nobody's home."

Cheshire Police confirmed investigations were ongoing into the burglary but no arrests had been made.

articles.title: Boy showcases his 'tiny gallery' of artworks in Melton Mowbray
articles.summary: Max has curated his own miniature exhibition outside his Melton Mowbray home.
articles.body:
A boy who spent his summer holiday recreating works of art in miniature has put his creations on display to the public.

Max, seven, recreated works including the Mona Lisa and Vincent van Gogh's The Starry night for his "Tiny Gallery" which is being showcased outside his home in Leicestershire.

He said the idea for the theme of his gallery, which also features small croissants, French flags and paintings of the Eiffel Tower, came after a visit to Paris earlier this year.

Max said that next month, his pieces will be inspired by artist Andy Warhol. All items are up for sale, with proceeds going to The Air Ambulance Service.

Max, who is neurodivergent, said the idea to create a miniature gallery came from visiting "lots of cake sheds" near the family's home in Melton Mowbray.

"My mummy and I like art and she takes me to see lots of exhibitions and does art activities with me," he said.

"There was an art competition at my school, and I did some colourful pieces. So, I thought I could use some for my first exhibition.

"I also made some mosaic, inspired by French art. My daddy built the tiny gallery box."

Max said he was "happy and excited" that people had seen his gallery and had donated more than £165 to charity so far.

"I'm raising money for The Air Ambulance Service because they are really important in helping people," he added.

Max's mother Laura, 39, said: "Max kept asking me if we could open our own cake shed and I was like, 'Baking's not really my thing'.

"He really loved the idea of having a tiny gallery on the front garden and raising money for charity.

"It's been really nice to collaborate with him and have a thing that's both our passion and get to work on together."

Laura said Max had chosen all the themes for each month, adding they have all been "inspired off things that Max has seen and what Max loves".

"We went to Paris in February, we went to the Louvre Museum and saw the real Mona Lisa. Max absolutely loved it," she said.

Laura added: "Then we went to see the Andy Warhol exhibition in Nottingham recently.

"It makes me really proud of what he's done and the fact that he's done it all for charity."

She said the exhibition has been "super popular" with the community.

"It's been really nice to have support from the local community, from our friends, our neighbours and lots of people that we don't know as well," she added.

"They have come and bought something, they've supported the charity and supported Max and his gallery."

The Air Ambulance Service provides emergency care across Leicestershire, Rutland, Warwickshire, Northamptonshire and Derbyshire.

articles.title: 'I turned heartbreak into starting an amazing travel club'
articles.summary: Emma Hickman started the travel firm 12 years ago after feeling isolated following a break-up.
articles.body:
A woman from Kenilworth who started a travel firm giving solo travellers the chance to travel with others says it has now grown to have 15,000 members across the UK.

Emma Hickman, 47, started the firm 'Travel Buddies Holidays' 12 years ago after splitting from her boyfriend at the time. She said her daughter had a baby, and she was left feeling "isolated and lonely".

Hickman said she wanted to go out and enjoy herself, but friends and family were either not in the same circumstance, could not get time off work, had families or different financial situations.

"When I split up from my partner, I was looking for ideas for social groups and that is what made me create the travel club," she said.

The first trip was trip was to the Lake District with 10 people, and now the firm takes groups of people to different destinations around the world. It even has international clients.

"One time a guy went on a cruise in Greece but couldn't swim, but all the girls taught him how to, and he sent me an email saying thank you," she said.

Hickman added that the firm is "really beneficial to so many people for many reasons".

"I think a lot of people [think] if they get divorced, or their partner has an affair, or passes away, it's very easy to feel that you are very isolated and have the whole weight of world on your shoulders – but then you find out that everyone has something going on.

"It's a case of coming together, encouraging each other and supporting each other."

Hickman said she has met friends for her life, her mum is one of the tour leaders and her daughter works in their office in Kenilworth.

She even met her now-husband in March 2023 on one of the group holidays in Jordan.

"A lot of my clients do say that they are happy travelling solo but the hardest part they find is eating on their own in restaurants in the evenings – we arrange group meals every evening and people can come along if they want to."

Hickman said people have made new friends on their holiday trips and go away together.

"One of the loveliest comments from my members was a lady who said it was like travelling with friends you didn't know you had," she added.

The firm runs tours with around 12 people per group as well as a tour leader.

"Experiences are much better shared, there is certainly a need for it and it has been an absolutely wonderful journey," she added.

articles.title: Cheltenham artist explores 'beautiful mess' of motherhood
articles.summary: A woman who had a baby through IVF is looking at the challenges of motherhood in a new exhibition.
articles.body:
An artist who spent years trying to have a baby through IVF has created an exhibition exploring motherhood.

Emma Howell, 34, from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, gave birth to her daughter in February 2025 after what she described as a "gruelling" IVF process.

Her exhibition, Day after Day, looks at the first 18 months of motherhood through four seasons: Overstimulation, endurance, lessons and becoming.

"It's beautiful, it's wonderful, it's all of those words, but it's also full of grit and sadness and jealousy of the old life," she said.

Howell said her experience of infertility and IVF had consumed her identity, leaving her with complex emotions that she was still trying to process.

"It overtakes every ounce of your being and just the waiting and the phone calls and the tests and it just completely consumes you."

She said that, despite wanting a child for so long, she had not been prepared for the reality of motherhood.

"Up until the day she was born, it was almost kind of disbelief. It's denial. It's constant denial.

"And when she was born, did I have that overwhelming sense of rush of love?

"No, I didn't, because I was just so scared about what's next.

"And obviously I was so focused on the infertility and actually getting pregnant, the having the baby bit I didn't even think about."

After wanting a baby for so long, Howell said she felt an "overwhelming sense of guilt" through the difficult times.

"She cried all day, she kind of had colicky episodes for the first six months.

"I still, to this day, have hard days, and I think maybe was the universe telling me I shouldn't have been a mother?"

She said motherhood had also changed her understanding of identity.

"Everyone always puts pressure on, once you have a baby, get back to the old you.

"But there is no old, that person is gone."

But Howell said her daughter was "very active, lovely and happy."

Howell's exhibition explores the passing of time, with the days of early motherhood often feeling repetitive while huge changes take place.

The title Day after Day also has a personal meaning for Howell, abbreviating to DAD in honour of her father, Mark Howell, a local musician who died 10 years ago.

"He will always be woven into all of my artwork. He was a creative person, a musician. My pursuit in his life is to just continue his legacy. It just feels like a kind of inner calling, so painting isn't really optional for me."

Day after Day is on display at Sixteen Gallery in Montpellier, Cheltenham, from 25-30 September.

articles.title: Northern Ireland court allows Orange Order march through Catholic area
articles.summary: Crowd gathers on Garvaghy Road early on Sunday morning to protest against the ruling allowing the march.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland’s High Court has permitted the Orange Order, a Protestant organisation, to march through a mainly Catholic area in the town of Portadown for the first time in 28 years, reviving one of the region’s most contentious marching disputes.

The court rejected a final attempt by residents to stop the parade passing through the Garvaghy Road early on Sunday, after Northern Ireland’s Court of Appeal overturned a temporary injunction granted on Saturday.

Large crowds gathered on the road before the procession, with the Belfast Telegraph reporting that protesters planned to block the route peacefully by linking arms.

First Minister Michelle O’Neill, vice president of Sinn Fein, an Irish nationalist party that supports a united Ireland, joined residents opposing the march.

In a statement posted on X on Sunday, she backed their right to protest and urged restraint, saying, “I am calling for calm on all sides.”

Sinn Fein leader Mary Lou McDonald also condemned the court decision in a post on X early on Sunday, calling it “disgraceful” and saying her party stood with the Garvaghy Road community.

Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), which supports Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, urged people to stay away from the area.

She said on Sunday that threats of violence were unacceptable and added: “No one in Northern Ireland wants violence or disorder.”

The Orange Order is a Protestant organisation closely associated with unionism, the political tradition that favours Northern Ireland remaining in the UK.

The Parades Commission, the independent body that rules on disputed marches in Northern Ireland, approved Sunday’s procession with a 35-person limit, barred bands and accompanying supporters, and required the march to finish by 9:30am (08:30 GMT).

The dispute over the Drumcree parade and Garvaghy Road became one of the most bitter marching confrontations of the “Troubles”, the decades-long conflict over Northern Ireland’s political status that largely ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.

Repeated attempts by the Orange Order to return from Drumcree church along Garvaghy Road triggered protests, violence and major security operations during the 1990s.

articles.title: Six missing in avalanche as severe weather batters Nepal
articles.summary: At least six people are missing in Nepal after an avalanche hit base camp at a remote mountain where climbers and support staff were preparing for an expedition, according to organizers.
articles.body: At least six people are missing in Nepal after an avalanche hit base camp at a remote mountain where climbers and support staff were preparing for an expedition, according to organizers. Sherpas and kitchen staff were fixing ropes and setting up tents at the Himlung Himal base camp in central Nepal for a group from the United Arab Emirates set to arrive on October 1, when a torrent of snow and rock swept down the mountainside. It comes just weeks after the catastrophic flooding disaster on the Nepal-China border that was sparked by a huge glacier collapse and landslide, which killed at least 1,300 people and left more than 5,000 missing. Nepal, which relies heavily on tourism, has been urging international visitors not to cancel their trips despite the devastation. Sunday’s avalanche comes with severe weather warnings in place for some parts of the Himalayan nation. The National Trust for Nature Conservation recently suspended entry permits to the Annapurna and Manaslu conservation areas, home to some of Nepal’s most popular trekking routes, from September 24 to 26 due to heavy rainfall. The Himlung Himal mountain, reaching 7,126 meters (23,000 feet), is part of this region, near the China border. At least six Nepalis who were at the base camp are missing, according to Barun Bhandari, general manager of Himalayan Holidays, the company organizing the expedition. “We are very devastated,” he told CNN. “We heard this morning that six or seven of our crew is missing but we are yet to confirm the exact number. “This is the first time we have had an avalanche like this in this exact area. “The ground is very flat at the base camp so we are quite surprised. But you never know, the mountain is unpredictable.” Renowned climber Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, owner of another company running an expedition on the mountain, told CNN two of his kitchen staff are among the missing. Bhandari said the company is working with Nepal’s tourism board to confirm the exact number of people missing on the mountain, and is working to send a rescue helicopter to the base camp. But rainfall remains heavy in the area and lines of communication are limited, due to its remoteness. The team – Sherpas, kitchen staff and general crew – had reached the base camp safely on September 18 carrying food and climbing equipment, Bhandari said. “They have been there setting up tents, fixing ropes for the climb, monitoring the conditions on the mountain and setting up the kitchen.” CNN has contacted the Nepal Tourism Board and local rescue groups for further information.

articles.title: Spain housing crisis: Thousands demand tenant protections after 87-year-old evicted  from Madrid home
articles.summary: Madrid’s housing crisis spilled onto the streets once again on Saturday (local time), as tens of thousands of people demanded greater protection for
articles.body: Madrid’s housing crisis spilled onto the streets once again on Saturday (local time), as tens of thousands of people demanded greater protection for tenants. Marching through the capital city, protesters called for measures against fraud, stronger safeguards for renters and a ban on evictions when no alternative housing is available.The demands were once again brought to light by the recent eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, who was forced out of her Madrid apartment on Wednesday after living there for decades.“We’re here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes,” said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse.“And we can’t keep maintaining this. Housing is a right and we don’t have it.”From 500 to 1,650 euros: When rent became unaffordable Abascal’s housing battle stretches back several years.Spanish media reported that her father first rented the apartment in 1956, and she remained there after her parents died. At the time, the property was covered by a rent cap.That changed after the building changed ownership in 2018. According to the Madrid Tenants’ Union, Abascal was offered the chance to buy the apartment but could not afford it.Urbagestión, an investment fund that later acquired the unit, increased her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros. The rent was subsequently reduced to 1,650 euros, but the amount was still beyond what Abascal could pay from her pension, the union said.Three earlier attempts to evict her were blocked by courts.Her eventual eviction on Wednesday drew extensive media attention and turned the 87-year-old into a symbol of the country's wider housing crisis.‘The last straw’For protesters, Abascal’s case reflected a much broader problem involving the cost and availability of housing.“This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we’ve been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now,” said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.“It’s unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can’t afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted.”The march later reached Madrid’s Puerta del Sol plaza, where protesters sat down and appeared intent on staying. Some pitched tents, planning to spend at least the night there or remain until police removed them.Spain’s housing shortage adds to pressureThe protest comes against a backdrop of rising housing costs and a shortage of homes that is pricing many Spaniards out of the market.Spain has recorded strong economic growth, but incomes have not kept pace with housing costs. Analysts have also pointed to tourism and population growth driven by immigration in cities as factors putting additional pressure on the country’s limited housing supply.The Bank of Spain estimated that Spain was short of about 550,000 homes last year. Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounted for a substantial share of the shortage.Public rental housing is also limited. Spain ranks near the bottom among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries, with public rental housing making up less than 2% of its available supply. The European Union average is 8%.Spain had previously used public funds to build homes that were subsequently sold into private ownership, removing those properties from the public housing stock.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: NCMC card mandatory for senior citizens, women passengers on MSRTC buses from October 1
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC) has announced that from October 1, the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) will be
articles.body: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC) has announced that from October 1, the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) will be mandatory for senior citizens, Amrit senior citizens and women passengers availing themselves of various fare concession schemes. The move aims to streamline and digitise travel concessions on state transport buses.Card registration and distribution have already begun at bus stations and depots across the state. Passengers who have an active NCMC card or a registration receipt with a QR code will be eligible for discounted tickets. For those awaiting their physical cards, the QR code-enabled registration receipt will remain valid for 30 days when scanned on the conductor's Electronic Ticketing Machine (ETM). During this period, passengers must activate and top up their NCMC cards.MSRTC has partnered with E-Bix Technologies Limited as the authorised agency to manage card registration at bus stands and designated centres. Passengers can top up their cards by scanning the QR code on the back using the BHIM app.Alternative provisions have also been introduced for beneficiaries who face difficulties with biometric fingerprint authentication on their identity cards. They can complete the registration process using an OTP sent to their linked mobile number.MSRTC has urged all eligible senior citizens and women passengers to complete their NCMC registration before October 1 to ensure uninterrupted, transparent and hassle-free travel.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Men held under Explosives Act as major incident declared
articles.summary: A major incident is declared and villagers have been evacuated from their homes in Whelford near RAF Fairford.
articles.body:
A major incident has been declared and homes have been evacuated in a village near an RAF base which hosts the United States Air Force.

Gloucestershire Police said residents in Whelford, near RAF Fairford, have been taken to a leisure centre while investigations continue.

Several men have been arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, police said.

The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team is currently examining a number of vehicles.

Police said a cordon was currently in place in the area and added officers believed the incident was contained.

A large emergency services presence was seen in the area, including a Hazardous Area Response Team.

Gloucestershire Police said: "A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident.

"It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.

"We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place."

The base has been used to deploy US bombers since the conflict in Iran began on 28 February.

Police said the men were arrested early on Sunday morning.

articles.title: Jamia’s first PG dental surgery batch asked to sign no-strike undertaking
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Candidates allotted seats in Jamia Millia Islamia’s first batch of Master of Dental Surgery (MDS) this year are being asked to sign an
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Candidates allotted seats in Jamia Millia Islamia’s first batch of Master of Dental Surgery (MDS) this year are being asked to sign an undertaking that prohibits them from participating in or associating themselves with any strike or activity deemed “prejudicial to the interests, discipline, peace and functioning” of the university.The undertaking, which is part of the documents required for completing admission formalities, comes alongside a Rs 10-lakh bond that MDS students are required to furnish if they leave the course midway. The bond requires the student and the surety to pay Rs 10 lakh, with 15% interest till realisation, if the student withdraws from the course “for any reason whatsoever”.Jamia, however, said the undertaking “will have no bearing” on admission. The university said MDS seats were being allotted through counselling by Medical Counselling Committee (MCC) on the basis of NEET-MDS merit and the undertaking was merely an admission formality. “In case someone does not sign the undertaking, it does not mean that admission will not be granted as seats are allotted by MCC,” chief public relations officer Saima Saeed told TOI.The bond, Saeed said, is intended to compensate for the public investment in infrastructure, faculty, manpower and clinical resources and the loss of a PG seat once the programme has commenced. It is intended to ensure that scarce MDS seats are utilised responsibly, she added.However, Jamia’s newly framed ordinance for the course, approved by its executive council in June, says admissions will be in accordance with the rules prescribed by National Dental Commission (NDC) and the university. The undertaking and bond are among the documents prescribed by the ordinance, but NDC doesn’t ask for them.Explaining the no-strike clause, Saeed said it was intended to maintain academic discipline in the demanding postgraduate programme. “As these are rigorous courses, attendance is a major requirement and indulging in protest, etc., can impact that. That clause is there to ensure general discipline and maintain a cordial and healthy environment,” she said.Jamia claimed that no other course had a no-strike clause. Its Bachelor of Dental Surgery students, however, are required to furnish a Rs 3-lakh discontinuation bond.Such bonds are also introduced by several other institutions. Maulana Azad Dental College has a Rs 10-lakh bond, while Aligarh Muslim University and Banaras Hindu University have bonds of Rs 8 lakh and Rs 5 lakh, respectively.The PG programme is a sought-after choice among candidates appearing for the highly competitive NEET-MDS examination, Jamia said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Photos: Heavy rains and flooding in Bangkok force thousands into shelters
articles.summary: Continuous downpours have hammered several areas of Thailand’s capital.
articles.body:
Flooding triggered by days of heavy rain in Thailand’s capital, Bangkok, has inundated homes and roads, affecting some 52,000 households, with nearly 4,900 people evacuated to shelters.

Water levels in the city’s network of canals remained high on Sunday morning, with authorities working to speed up drainage, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) said. More rain was forecast throughout Sunday for Bangkok and its surrounding provinces, but it would begin to taper off on Monday, it said.

Authorities declared a flood disaster across Bangkok on Saturday after almost 48 hours of heavy rain. More than 330mm (13 inches) of rain fell in some areas of the city between Thursday and Sunday, according to the weather agency.

Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to heat up because of fossil fuel emissions.

articles.title: Several arrested on suspicion of explosives offensives near UK air base used by US forces
articles.summary: Police in western England say several men have been arrested on suspicion of explosives offensives near an air base often used by US forces.
articles.body: Police in western England say several men have been arrested on suspicion of explosives offensives near an air base often used by US forces. A number of properties have been evacuated in the Whelford area of Gloucestershire, southern England, “following the declaration of a major incident,” a police statement said. Whelford is close to the Royal Air Force base at Fairford. “The Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles. The local residents are being evacuated to a nearby leisure centre,” the statement said “A cordon is currently in place but we’d like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained,” Gloucestershire police said.
